pos: n. (the oldest German city and archbishop-electorate, where Priscillian was executed in 385 and where the Holy Coat was exhibited)
etymology: From Latin Augusta Treverorum, the Augustan city of the Treveri, a Belgic people.
biblical_def: Trier on the Moselle is the oldest city in Germany, an imperial residence under Constantine, and from the Middle Ages an archbishopric whose holder was one of the seven electors of the Empire. Two things bring it into this dictionary. In 385 the Spanish bishop Priscillian was tried at Trier before the usurper Magnus Maximus and beheaded with six companions, the first execution for heresy carried out by a Christian state; Ambrose of Milan and Martin of Tours both refused communion with the bishops who had procured it. And the cathedral holds the Holy Coat, a garment exhibited as the seamless robe of Christ, shown publicly from 1512 and drawing enormous pilgrimages, including one in 1844 which provoked the German Catholic schism under Johannes Ronge. The dictionary records Trier for the execution above all. The date 385 is the hinge of an argument that ran for twelve hundred years, and the two men who protested it were the two most respected bishops in the West.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an elector as one who has the right of choosing an emperor; heresy as a fundamental error in religion; a usurper as one who seizes power unlawfully; a relic as the remains of a saint; and communion as fellowship in the church.
webster_full: ELECTOR, n. One who elects, or one who has the right of choice; a prince who had a voice in the choice of the German emperor.
HERESY, n. A fundamental error in religion, or an error of opinion respecting some fundamental doctrine of religion.
USURPER, n. One who seizes power or possessions without right; one who dispossesses the lawful ruler.
RELIC, n. The remains of the body of a saint, or something belonging to a saint, preserved with great respect as a sacred memorial.
COMMUNION, n. Fellowship; intercourse; mutual participation in the Lord's supper; the body of christians who have one common faith.
scriptures: Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.
Tit 3:10
A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject;
(For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)

Let both grow together until the harvest: and in the time of harvest I will say to the reapers, Gather ye together first the tares, and bind them in bundles to burn them: but gather the wheat into my barn.
corruption_summary: Oldest German city and archbishop-electorate where Priscillian was beheaded in 385, the first execution for heresy by a Christian state.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the death penalty for heresy, and the dictionary names 385 as the year the church accepted it and the twelve centuries that followed as the consequence. Christ's word to Peter in the garden settles the method for his servants, and it is given in a situation where the cause was unarguably just: “Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Mat 26:52). Paul's instruction about a factious man stops at exclusion, “A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject” (Tit 3:10).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is the patience Christ requires with a mixed field. The command is explicit about the timing and about who executes the separation: “Let both grow together until the harvest” (Mat 13:30). The church's own armoury is named and it contains nothing of steel, since “the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds” (2Co 10:4). The dictionary records with respect that Ambrose and Martin broke communion with the bishops responsible at Trier, and holds that their judgment, not the tribunal's, was the mind of the church.

pos: n. (the Rhenish duchy of Julich-Cleves-Berg whose Erasmian church order sought a middle way, and whose disputed succession opened the Thirty Years' War's prelude)
etymology: From Latin Juliacum, a Roman station on the road from Cologne to Tongeren; the German form is Jülich.
biblical_def: Juliers is the French and English name of Julich, a small duchy on the Rhine which in 1521 was united with Cleves, Berg and Mark under Duke John the Third and became the largest territory of the Lower Rhine. Its church policy under John and his son William the Fifth was deliberately Erasmian: a church order of 1532 and 1533 which kept the old liturgy and hierarchy while introducing preaching, catechising, a vernacular element and the abolition of the worst abuses, and which punished both Lutheran and Roman partisans for disturbing the peace. It satisfied nobody for long. When the last duke died insane and childless in 1609 the succession was disputed between Brandenburg and the Palatinate-Neuburg, Catholic and Protestant powers intervened, and the crisis of 1609 to 1614 was the rehearsal for the Thirty Years' War. The dictionary records Juliers as the best-documented attempt at a confessional middle way, and as evidence that such a policy postpones a decision rather than resolving it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a compromise as a mutual promise to abide by an award; neutrality as a state of indifference; a succession as the order of coming after; moderation as restraint of violent passions; and indifference as neutrality of mind.
webster_full: COMPROMISE, n. A mutual promise or contract of two parties in controversy, to refer their differences to the decision of arbitrators.
NEUTRALITY, n. A state of indifference, or of neither friendship nor hostility; the condition of a nation which takes no part in a contest.
SUCCESSION, n. A following of things in order; the act of succeeding or coming in the place of another; lineage.
MODERATION, n. Restraint of violent passions or indulgence of appetite; calmness of mind; equanimity.
INDIFFERENCE, n. Neutrality of mind between different persons or things; a state in which there is no special inclination.
scriptures: Rev 3:16
So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth.
And Elijah came unto all the people, and said, How long halt ye between two opinions? if the LORD be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him. And the people answered him not a word.
Mat 6:24
No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon.

And if it seem evil unto you to serve the LORD, choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.
corruption_summary: Rhenish duchy whose Erasmian church order of the fifteen-thirties sought a confessional middle way, and whose disputed succession of 1609 rehearsed the Thirty Years' War.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the confessional middle way treated as a permanent settlement rather than as a delay. The dictionary grants the attraction: the dukes of Juliers wanted preaching and catechising without a schism, and their subjects were spared a generation of violence. But the question at issue was how a sinner is accepted, which admits no middle, and the Lord's word to a church that had found one is the sharpest in the Revelation: “So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth” (Rev 3:16).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover. Elijah's challenge on Carmel assumes that a divided people is in an unbearable position and must be made to answer, demanding “How long halt ye between two opinions?” (1Ki 18:21), and Christ denies the possibility of a double allegiance outright: “No man can serve two masters” (Mat 6:24). Joshua puts the decision in the only form that settles anything, household by household and dated: “choose you this day whom ye will serve” (Jos 24:15). The dictionary adds the historical point. The duchy's middle way lasted eighty years and then its succession dispute helped start the worst war in German history.

pos: n. (the Westphalian see where the Protestant half of the Peace of Westphalia was negotiated in 1648, and which afterwards alternated Catholic and Lutheran bishops)
etymology: From Old Saxon Osnabrugge, the bridge over the Hase or Osna, from brugge, a bridge.
biblical_def: Osnabruck is a Westphalian city and see founded by Charlemagne. In the negotiations that ended the Thirty Years' War the imperial delegation dealt with the Swedes and the Protestant estates at Osnabruck and with France and the Catholic estates at Munster, and the two treaties signed on the twenty-fourth of October 1648 together make the Peace of Westphalia. The settlement recognised Calvinism alongside Lutheranism and Catholicism, fixed 1624 as the normative year for confessional possession, gave subjects whose ruler changed religion the right to emigrate, and made the Empire's religious constitution a matter of treaty rather than of victory. Osnabruck itself received a unique arrangement: its bishopric was thereafter held alternately by a Catholic bishop and a Lutheran prince of the house of Brunswick. The dictionary records Osnabruck as the point at which Europe gave up trying to settle doctrine by war, which is a real gain, and began to treat confession as a matter of territory, which is not the same as liberty of conscience.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a treaty as an agreement between nations; peace as freedom from war; a plenipotentiary as a person with full power; toleration as the allowance of religious opinions; and emigration as the removal from one country to another.
webster_full: TREATY, n. An agreement, league or contract between two or more nations or sovereigns, formally signed by commissioners.
PEACE, n. In a general sense, a state of quiet or tranquillity; freedom from war with a foreign nation; public quiet.
PLENIPOTENTIARY, n. A person vested with full power to transact any business; particularly, an ambassador or envoy.
TOLERATION, n. The allowance of that which is not wholly approved; allowance of religious opinions and modes of worship in a state.
EMIGRATION, n. The act of removing from one country or state to another, for the purpose of residence.
scriptures: Mat 5:9
Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.
Let us therefore follow after the things which make for peace, and things wherewith one may edify another.
Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord:
Rom 13:4

For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
corruption_summary: Westphalian see where the Protestant half of the 1648 Peace of Westphalia was negotiated, afterwards held alternately by Catholic and Lutheran bishops.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that peace-making is a Christian work and not a compromise of truth. Thirty years of war had killed perhaps a third of the German population over questions that no army was ever going to decide, and the men who stopped it deserve the beatitude: “Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God” (Mat 5:9). Paul makes the pursuit a standing duty where brethren differ, “Let us therefore follow after the things which make for peace” (Rom 14:19).

The second paragraph names the live temptation, which is to mistake Westphalia for religious liberty. It was not. It settled whose confession would be established in whose territory and allowed dissenters to leave; a man's conscience was still his prince's business. The dictionary holds that the magistrate has a real office, “for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil” (Rom 13:4), and that the office does not extend to prescribing a man's faith. What Scripture asks of believers under any such settlement is the double pursuit: “Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord” (Heb 12:14).

pos: n. (the Westphalian see founded by Charlemagne at the assembly of 777, where the Saxons were received to baptism under the threat of death)
etymology: From Old High German Pader, the river, and born, a spring.
biblical_def: Paderborn in eastern Westphalia is where Charlemagne held the imperial assembly of 777 at which Saxon nobles submitted and were baptised, and where in 799 he met Pope Leo the Third. The bishopric was founded about 806 as part of the settlement of Saxony. The terms of that settlement are preserved in the capitulary for Saxony, which prescribed death for refusing baptism, for eating meat in Lent, for burning a church, and for sacrificing to the old gods; Alcuin of York wrote to Charlemagne objecting that faith must be voluntary and that tithes should not be exacted from new converts. Paderborn was later a centre of the Catholic Reformation with a Jesuit university from 1614. The dictionary records Paderborn for the capitulary and for Alcuin's letters, which are the earliest sustained argument in Western Christendom that compulsion cannot make a Christian, written by a man at the centre of the court that was doing the compelling.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a capitulary as a collection of laws or ordinances; compulsion as the act of driving by force; voluntary as proceeding from one's own choice; a tithe as the tenth part; and persuasion as the act of influencing by argument.
webster_full: CAPITULARY, n. The body of laws or statutes of a chapter, or of an ecclesiastical council; the laws of Charlemagne and other princes.
COMPULSION, n. The act of driving or urging by force, physical or moral; force applied; constraint of the will.
VOLUNTARY, a. Acting by choice or spontaneously; proceeding from choice or free will; not constrained.
TITHE, n. The tenth part of any thing; the tenth part of the annual produce of land, allotted to the clergy.
PERSUASION, n. The act of persuading; the act of influencing the mind by arguments or reasons offered, or by motives.
scriptures: So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.
Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men; but we are made manifest unto God; and I trust also are made manifest in your consciences.
Act 18:4
And he reasoned in the synagogue every sabbath, and persuaded the Jews and the Greeks.
For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.
corruption_summary: Westphalian see founded in the settlement of Saxony, where the capitulary prescribed death for refusing baptism and Alcuin objected that faith must be voluntary.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is baptism under threat of death, which Charlemagne's Saxon capitulary explicitly commanded, and the dictionary names the objection as having been raised at the time by the best scholar at his court. Alcuin's argument was simply that of the New Testament. Faith arises from hearing and not from force: “So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17), and the thing required of a convert is interior, “For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness” (Rom 10:10).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is persuasion as the apostolic method. Paul describes his own ministry in exactly those terms, “Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men” (2Co 5:11), and Luke records the ordinary pattern of his work as argument in a public place week by week: he “reasoned in the synagogue every sabbath, and persuaded the Jews and the Greeks” (Act 18:4). The dictionary adds that the Saxon mission did eventually produce genuine Christianity in Westphalia, by schools and preaching over generations, and that none of that was owing to the article of the capitulary which made unbaptism a capital crime.

pos: n. (the Westphalian see on the Weser which adopted the Reformation in 1530 and was secularised to Brandenburg in 1648)
etymology: From Old Saxon Mimidun, of uncertain sense, perhaps from a personal name and dun, a hill.
biblical_def: Minden stands where the Weser cuts through the hills at the Porta Westfalica, and its see was founded by Charlemagne about 803. The city adopted the Reformation in 1530 under the influence of Nicolaus Krage and the Brunswick church orders, and its citizens worked out a Lutheran church ordinance while the prince-bishop remained Catholic, so that the bishopric and the town were of different confessions for over a century, with repeated disputes over churches and revenues. By the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 the bishopric was secularised and given to Brandenburg as a principality, which ended the arrangement by abolishing the office. The dictionary records Minden as the ordinary German case: a town that reformed itself and a prelate who did not, living alongside each other with lawsuits instead of massacres. Most of the Reformation in Germany was this, not Worms and not Munster, and the dictionary says so because a reader who knows only the famous scenes will have the wrong impression of how the thing actually happened.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines secularisation as the conversion of a religious office to lay use; an ordinance as a rule established by authority; a burgher as an inhabitant of a borough; revenue as the annual income of an estate; and a magistrate as a public civil officer.
webster_full: SECULARIZE, v.t. To make secular; to convert from spiritual appropriation to secular or common use.
ORDINANCE, n. A rule established by authority; a permanent rule of action; an established rite or ceremony.
BURGHER, n. An inhabitant of a borough or walled town, or one who possesses a privilege of trading there.
REVENUE, n. The annual rents, profits, interest or issues of any species of property; the income of a church or a state.
MAGISTRATE, n. A public civil officer, invested with the executive government or some branch of it.
scriptures: Let all things be done decently and in order.
For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things;
If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.
Tit 1:5
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
corruption_summary: Westphalian see on the Weser whose town adopted the Reformation in 1530 while its prince-bishop remained Catholic, and which was secularised to Brandenburg in 1648.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the quiet, legal, institutional form of reformation, which is how most of it actually happened. A city council, a preacher and a printed church order did more across northern Germany than any battle, and Scripture gives the instinct behind that work in a single clause: “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40). Paul left Titus in Crete for exactly this, “that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5).

The second paragraph names the live temptation, which is impatience with the slow forms. Minden and its bishop coexisted for a hundred and eighteen years with disputes over buildings and tithes, and that is a better record than Munster's eighteen months. The apostolic letter from Jerusalem is the model of a church settling a hard question by a written order with reasons, “For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden” (Act 15:28), and Paul makes peaceableness a command with a realistic limit built in: “If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men” (Rom 12:18).

pos: n. (the Lower Saxon see whose city turned Lutheran in 1542 while the bishopric remained Catholic, and whose cathedral keeps the thousand-year rose)
etymology: From Old High German Hildin, a personal name, and heim, a home.
biblical_def: Hildesheim was founded as a see by Louis the Pious in 815 and its cathedral is famous for the bronze doors and column of Bishop Bernward and for a rose bush growing against the apse, traditionally dated to the foundation and still alive, which survived the destruction of the cathedral by bombing in 1945 and flowered again the next year. The diocesan feud of 1519 to 1523 broke the bishopric's power and cost it most of its territory. The city adopted the Reformation in 1542 through a church order drawn up with Johannes Bugenhagen's help, while the bishopric remained Catholic, so that here as at Minden two confessions shared a cathedral close for generations. The dictionary records Hildesheim for the rose, as a figure rather than a relic. A root that outlives the building above it is what the church is, and the dictionary says plainly that the figure is an illustration and not a sign, which is the distinction a thousand years of relic devotion failed to keep.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a root as the part of a plant which enters the earth; a figure as a type or representation; a remnant as that which is left; endurance as continuance under suffering; and a type as an emblem or figure of something future.
webster_full: ROOT, n. That part of a plant which enters and fixes itself in the earth, and serves to support the plant and supply it with nourishment.
FIGURE, n. In rhetoric, a mode of speaking or writing in which words are deflected from their ordinary signification; a type.
REMNANT, n. Residue; that which is left after the separation, removal or destruction of a part.
ENDURANCE, n. Continuance; a bearing or suffering; a state of enduring pain or distress.
TYPE, n. The mark of something; an emblem; that which represents something future; a figure or representation.
scriptures: Job 14:7
For there is hope of a tree, if it be cut down, that it will sprout again, and that the tender branch thereof will not cease.
Isa 11:1
And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots:
For if the firstfruit be holy, the lump is also holy: and if the root be holy, so are the branches.
Psa 1:3
And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither; and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper.
corruption_summary: Lower Saxon see whose city adopted the Reformation in 1542 while the bishopric remained Catholic, and whose cathedral keeps a rose bush traditionally dated to its foundation.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the difference between a figure and a relic. The Hildesheim rose is an illustration of something true, that a root may outlast the building: “For there is hope of a tree, if it be cut down, that it will sprout again” (Job 14:7). A figure instructs and may be admired. A relic is venerated, and the whole medieval apparatus grew from treating the second category as though it were the first.

The second paragraph names the live temptation and states the doctrine the figure illustrates. Isaiah's picture of the Messiah is exactly this image applied to a cut-down dynasty, “And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots” (Isa 11:1); Paul uses the root to establish that the believing remnant carries the whole, “For if the firstfruit be holy, the lump is also holy: and if the root be holy, so are the branches” (Rom 11:16); and the psalmist describes the man who is planted rather than merely busy: he “shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water” (Psa 1:3). The rose is a pleasant thing in a cathedral close. The doctrine is the point.

pos: n. (the Saxon see administered with Magdeburg and Mainz by Albert of Brandenburg, whose indulgence campaign of 1517 provoked the Ninety-five Theses)
etymology: From Old High German halb, half, and stat, a place; a settlement name of uncertain sense.
biblical_def: Halberstadt is a Saxon see founded about 804 whose cathedral and treasury are among the richest in Germany. Its importance here is a transaction. In 1513 Albert of Brandenburg, aged twenty-three, was made bishop of Halberstadt and archbishop of Magdeburg at once; in 1514 he was additionally elected archbishop of Mainz, which required a papal dispensation for holding three sees. He borrowed the enormous fee from the Fugger bank and was granted, in return, the right to preach in his territories the indulgence for the rebuilding of Saint Peter's, with half the proceeds going to repay his debt. Johann Tetzel was his commissioner. The Ninety-five Theses of October 1517 were a protest against that campaign, and Luther sent a copy to Albert. The dictionary records Halberstadt because the Reformation's first public act was occasioned by a financial instrument: a loan to buy church offices, serviced by the sale of pardons to peasants.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an indulgence as a remission of punishment granted by the pope; pluralism as the holding of more benefices than one; simony as the buying or selling of church preferment; a dispensation as a relaxation of law; and pardon as forgiveness.
webster_full: INDULGENCE, n. In the Romish church, remission of the punishment due to sins, granted by the pope or church, and supposed to save the sinner from purgatory.
PLURALITY, n. In the church of England, the holding of two or more benefices by the same clergyman at the same time.
SIMONY, n. The crime of buying or selling ecclesiastical preferment, or of corruptly presenting to a benefice.
DISPENSATION, n. The granting of a license, or the license itself, to do what is forbidden by laws or canons.
PARDON, n. Forgiveness; the remission of a penalty; remission of a sentence or punishment.

But Peter said unto him, Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money.
Isa 55:1
Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.
Rom 3:24
Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus:
Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
corruption_summary: Saxon see held with Magdeburg and Mainz by Albert of Brandenburg, whose Fugger loan was serviced by the 1517 indulgence campaign that provoked the Ninety-five Theses.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the sale of forgiveness, and Halberstadt supplies the whole chain: three sees held by one man of twenty-four, a dispensation bought with borrowed money, and a pardon-campaign in the same territories to repay the loan. Peter had already judged the transaction in its original form, when a man offered money for a spiritual gift: “But Peter said unto him, Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money” (Act 8:20). The word for that offence is taken from the man's name.

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is that the thing being sold is given. Isaiah's invitation is addressed to the penniless and makes the absence of money the condition of coming: “come, buy wine and milk without money and without price” (Isa 55:1). Paul states the mechanism as a gift and a purchase already made by another, “Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (Rom 3:24), and he blocks every contribution of our own: “For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God” (Eph 2:8). Halberstadt's treasury is still rich. What it sold was never its own.
roots_summary: Greek dorea (G1431), a gift; Greek charis (G5485), grace; Greek apolutrosis (G0629), redemption.
roots_lines: Greek dorea (G1431) — a free gift; “the gift of God may be purchased with money”, Acts 8:20.

“come, buy wine and milk without money and without price” (Isa 55:1) — the terms actually offered.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith” (Eph 2:8) — every contribution of our own blocked.

pos: n. (the Lower Saxon town where Charlemagne is recorded to have executed some four thousand five hundred Saxon captives in 782)
etymology: From Old Saxon Ferdi, perhaps a ford, with the locative ending; the German is Verden an der Aller.
biblical_def: Verden lies on the Aller in Lower Saxony and was made a see about 800. The royal Frankish annals record that in 782, after a Saxon rising in which a Frankish army was destroyed at the Suntel hills, Charlemagne came to Verden, demanded the surrender of those responsible, and had four thousand five hundred Saxons beheaded in one place. The number has been questioned and the text has been argued over, but no serious account removes the massacre. It was followed by the capitulary for Saxony with its death penalty for refusing baptism, and by the deportations that eventually broke Saxon resistance. Alcuin protested the whole policy from the court itself. The dictionary records Verden because the conversion of Saxony is the largest forced Christianisation in European history and the church has never squarely accounted for it, and because the only honest thing a Christian can say about four and a half thousand beheaded prisoners is that it was murder done in the name of Christ.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a massacre as the slaughter of numbers with cruelty; a captive as one taken in war; quarter as mercy granted to a surrendering enemy; vengeance as the infliction of pain in return for injury; and bloodguiltiness as the guilt of shedding blood.
webster_full: MASSACRE, n. The murder of an individual, or the slaughter of numbers of human beings, with cruelty or atrocity, or contrary to the usages of nations.
CAPTIVE, n. A prisoner taken by force or stratagem in war, by an enemy; one who is charmed or subdued by beauty or excellence.
QUARTER, n. Mercy granted by a conqueror to his enemy, when no longer able to defend himself; the sparing of life.
VENGEANCE, n. The infliction of pain on another, in return for an injury or offense; punishment inflicted in return for an injury.
BLOODGUILTINESS, n. The crime of shedding blood; the guilt of murder.
scriptures: Gen 9:6
Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man.
Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God, thou God of my salvation: and my tongue shall sing aloud of thy righteousness.
To me belongeth vengeance, and recompence; their foot shall slide in due time: for the day of their calamity is at hand, and the things that shall come upon them make haste.
Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.
corruption_summary: Lower Saxon town where the Frankish annals record the beheading of some four thousand five hundred Saxon captives in 782, in the campaign that forced Saxony's conversion.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the slaughter of prisoners by a Christian king with clergy in his train, and the dictionary names it without the usual mitigations. The law that governs it was given before Israel existed, to the whole race, and grounds itself in the image of God rather than in any covenant: “Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man” (Gen 9:6). The Saxons beheaded at Verden bore that image, and their paganism did not remove it.

The second paragraph names the principle to recover. Vengeance is reserved and is not delegated to kings pursuing a mission, “To me belongeth vengeance, and recompence” (Deu 32:35), and Christ's word in the garden forbids the sword to his servants in the one case where the cause was perfectly just: “all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Mat 26:52). The psalm supplies the only language in which a church that did this can speak afterwards, and it is confession rather than explanation: “Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God, thou God of my salvation” (Psa 51:14). The dictionary holds that Verden is owed that prayer and has never been given it.

“Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God” (Psa 51:14) — the only language left afterwards.

pos: n. (the Lower Saxon county which adopted the Reformation in 1573 and whose dynasty supplied the kings of Denmark, Norway, Sweden and Greece)
etymology: From Low German olde, old, and burg, a fortress.
biblical_def: Oldenburg is a county of the north German coastal plain between Bremen and Frisia, held by its own line of counts, which introduced the Reformation by a church order in 1573 under Count John the Seventh. Count Anton Gunther, ruling from 1603 to 1667, kept the county out of the Thirty Years' War entirely by diplomacy, by a toll on the Weser and by the judicious gift of horses, and it emerged undamaged while Lower Saxony around it was ruined. The house of Oldenburg, through the election of Christian the First to the Danish throne in 1448, supplied the kings of Denmark and Norway, later of Sweden and Greece, and the present dynasties of Denmark, Norway and the United Kingdom descend from it. The dictionary records Oldenburg for Anton Gunther, because a Christian ruler who keeps his people out of a war and is remembered as a horse-trader rather than a hero is nearer the pattern Scripture commends than most of the men who got statues.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines diplomacy as the art of conducting negotiations; neutrality as a state of taking no part in a contest; a toll as a tax for passage; a dynasty as a race of kings; and prudence as wisdom applied to practice.
webster_full: DIPLOMACY, n. The customs, rules and privileges of embassadors and other representatives of princes at foreign courts; forms of negotiation.
NEUTRALITY, n. The condition of a nation or state which takes no part in a contest between others; a state of indifference.
TOLL, n. A tax paid for some liberty or privilege, particularly for the privilege of passing over a bridge or on a highway.
DYNASTY, n. A race or succession of kings of the same line or family, who govern a particular country.
PRUDENCE, n. Wisdom applied to practice; that discretion which enables a person to judge what is best to be done or forborne.
scriptures: If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.
Mat 5:9
Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.
Pro 20:3
It is an honour for a man to cease from strife: but every fool will be meddling.
Jer 29:7
And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.
corruption_summary: Lower Saxon county which adopted the Reformation in 1573 and which its Count Anton Gunther kept out of the Thirty Years' War entirely by diplomacy.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that keeping a people out of a war is a Christian achievement and not a failure of nerve. Anton Gunther is usually a comic figure in the histories because he bought off armies with horses and a river toll, and the dictionary thinks the histories have the valuation backwards. Paul makes the duty explicit and attaches a limit that admits it is not always possible: “If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men” (Rom 12:18).

The second paragraph names the live temptation, which is the glorification of belligerence under the name of principle. Christ blesses a different trade: “Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God” (Mat 5:9). Solomon states the honour plainly and against the instinct of the age: “It is an honour for a man to cease from strife” (Pro 20:3). And Jeremiah's charge to exiles governs what a magistrate owes a people whose territory he holds, which is to seek its welfare rather than its glory: “seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives” (Jer 29:7).

pos: n. (the Saxon imperial abbey ruled by princess-abbesses, which adopted the Reformation in 1539 and remained a Lutheran women's foundation until 1803)
etymology: From Old High German Quitilinga, perhaps the people of Quitilo, with burg, a stronghold.
biblical_def: Quedlinburg in the Harz foreland was founded in 936 by Queen Mathilda as a house of canonesses on her husband Henry the Fowler's burial site, and its abbess held the rank of an imperial princess, sat in the Reichstag, coined money and governed the town. In 1539 Abbess Anna the Second of Stolberg introduced the Reformation, and the foundation continued as a Lutheran chapter of noblewomen, with a Lutheran abbess exercising the same temporal authority, until Prussia dissolved it in 1803. The town, which escaped the wars and later demolitions, keeps over a thousand timber-framed houses. The dictionary records Quedlinburg because it is the clearest instance of a women's institution surviving the Reformation by being reformed rather than suppressed, and because it raises in an acute form a question the dictionary answers plainly: a woman may hold property, govern a town, administer an estate and teach other women, and she may not hold the office of pastor or elder.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an abbess as the superior of a convent of nuns; a canoness as a woman living in a religious community without vows; a chapter as a society of clergymen; an estate as property in land; and an office as a public charge or trust.
webster_full: ABBESS, n. A female superior or governess of a nunnery or convent of nuns, having the same rights and authority over the nuns that the abbots have over the monks.
CANONESS, n. A woman who enjoys a prebend, affixed by the foundation to maids, without obliging them to renounce the world.
CHAPTER, n. A society or community of clergymen, belonging to a cathedral or collegiate church.
ESTATE, n. The interest or quantity of interest a man has in lands, tenements or other effects; property in land.
OFFICE, n. A particular duty, charge or trust conferred by public authority and for a public purpose; a place of trust.
scriptures: But I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man, but to be in silence.
Tit 2:4
That they may teach the young women to be sober, to love their husbands, to love their children,
She considereth a field, and buyeth it: with the fruit of her hands she planteth a vineyard.
And he began to speak boldly in the synagogue: whom when Aquila and Priscilla had heard, they took him unto them, and expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly.
corruption_summary: Saxon imperial abbey governed by princess-abbesses, reformed in 1539 under Anna the Second and continuing as a Lutheran women's foundation until 1803.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the modern collapse of two different questions into one, so that any limit on church office is read as a limit on a woman's capacity. Quedlinburg keeps them apart better than most modern argument does. Its abbess coined money, judged cases and sat among the princes of the Empire, and no Lutheran theologian thought she was therefore a pastor. The limit Paul sets is on one office and is stated in terms of teaching and authority in the assembly: “But I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man, but to be in silence” (1Ti 2:12).

The second paragraph names the positive side, which the dictionary insists is the larger half. Older women are commanded to teach, with a stated curriculum, “That they may teach the young women to be sober, to love their husbands, to love their children” (Tit 2:4); the capable woman of Proverbs buys land and plants on it, for “She considereth a field, and buyeth it: with the fruit of her hands she planteth a vineyard” (Pro 31:16); and Priscilla instructs an eloquent preacher in private alongside her husband, when “they took him unto them, and expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly” (Act 18:26). A reformed chapter of noblewomen governing a Harz town is well within all of that.
